## 1. How to Read the Figures

Figures are saved to `latest_visualization_<tag>_n<rows>/` (overwritten each
run — no history). A `figure_index.png` contact sheet shows all figures at a
glance; if any figure could not be generated, a red "FIGURE(S) NOT GENERATED
THIS RUN" block at the very **top** of the sheet lists each one with its
reason. Stable verification artifacts (snapshots, Bland-Altman plots,
threshold validation) live separately in `output/verification/<tag>/`.

**New to these figures?** Start with the `figure_index.png` contact sheet for
an overview, then work through the five "must-check" figures below in order —
together they are a sleep-quality QC pass in miniature. Every number below
(`F01`-`F37`) is the same number as the file name, the in-figure title and the
card in §4 or §5. The folder split (`pipeline_cleaning/` = QC/audit figures,
`research_ready/` = built for a paper) only matters once you are deciding what
to put in a manuscript — for just checking your data, ignore it and go by
number.

**Figure numbering, two systems.** `F01`-`F37` is the pipeline's own numbering:
file name, in-figure title, card heading and every cross-reference in this
documentation. The *paper* numbering is separate and exists only for a
manuscript: Methods Figure 1-2, Results Figure 3-13, Supplement Figure S1-S24.
The "Paper figure" column in the index (§3) maps one onto the other, and each
card's caption uses the paper number so it can be pasted into a manuscript
unchanged.

**Five must-check figures:**

| Step | Figure | Should look like | If not? |
|:----:|--------|------------------|---------|
| 1 | **F01** Pipeline Record Flow (§4) | Flow narrows gently; Clean dominates; Error + Unusual small (< 5%) | Spike at 0 or huge Error/Unusual share → parsing/AM-PM failure upstream |
| 2 | **F15** Step Flag Ledger (§4) | Corrected bar appears ONLY at Step 6.5, flat after | Change after Step 6.5 = instability |
| 3 | **F14** Auto-Detected Dashboard (§4) | Flag counts match `correction_status_final.csv` | Mismatch = misalignment |
| 4 | **F18** Distribution of Sleep Variables (§5) | TST peaks 6–8 h, SOL right-skewed, WASO < 60, SE > 85% | SOL flat/bimodal = AM/PM confusion |
| 5 | **F06** Error Category Distribution (§4) | Most records Clean/Minor; Error+Unusual < 5% | High = review the manual CSVs |

<a id="fr-2"></a>

## 2. What is in the output folder

The folder name is `latest_visualization_` + the dataset **tag** (`real`,
`synth`, …) + `_n` + the **number of input records** (for example
`latest_visualization_real_n13990` is a run on real data with 13,990 records).
It is rebuilt from scratch on every visualization run — it is "latest", not
"history". Copy anything you want to keep before rerunning. If the tag is
`real` it holds figures derived from participant data: it is gitignored, do not
commit or share it.

| Item | What it is | When to open it |
|------|-----------|-----------------|
| `pipeline_cleaning/` | 21 diagnostic figures: what the pipeline found and changed (cards in §4) | Checking that cleaning behaved; the audit trail for a supplement |
| `research_ready/` | 16 publication-oriented figures: sleep metrics, perception bias, substance use (cards in §5) | Choosing figures for Results |
| `figure_index.png` | One contact sheet of all figures. A red block at the top lists the figures that were skipped and why | First look after a run |
| `all_figures_review.pdf` | Every figure, one per page, in generation order, at the same size as the PNGs | Flipping through all figures quickly or sharing with a collaborator on the study team |
| `figures_not_generated.csv` | `file`, `reason`: each figure that was **not** produced and why (for example "fewer than 2 flag columns had complete data", or a validation file that was not found). Same list as the red block | A missing PNG: look here before suspecting a bug |
| `flag_distribution.csv` | One row per diary entry (`pid`, `day_num`, `row_id`) with its flag counts (`timestamp_flags`, `duration_flags`, `amount_flags`, `review_flags`), `flag_details`, `raw_category` and `final_status`, whether it was `manually_corrected`, and `data_category_after_corrections`. A manually corrected row is `CLEAN (Manually Fixed)` only when its Step 8 checks and its `data_category` both pass; with a Step 8 flag it keeps that flag, and with a failing `data_category` it is `STILL FAILS (Manually Corrected)` | The table behind the flag figures (F03, F06, F13, F14); filter it to find the entries behind a bar |
| `classification_summary.csv` | Counts per final classification (clean / error / unusual / …). Written only when the run produced a final classification | Cross-check with `correction_status_final.csv` (§4 of the [reading page](interpreting-output.html)) |
| `RUN_INFO.txt` | When the run was made, dataset tag, number of records, input file names, package version, where the verification files are | Recording which run a set of figures came from |

**The sibling folder `verification/<tag>_n<rows>/`** (next to this one, or
under `output/` for real data) is **not** wiped when the figures are rebuilt.
It holds the evidence used to check the pipeline, not figures for the paper:

| Item | What it is |
|------|-----------|
| `bland_altman_sol.png`, `bland_altman_waso.png` | Bland-Altman plots: agreement between self-reported and computed SOL / WASO |
| `threshold_validation.csv` | Each flagging threshold, the measurement noise (`loa_half_width`), their ratio and an assessment (for example "CONSERVATIVE", "SAFE") |
| `snapshot_*.rds` | Saved copies of the data at named points, used for the regression comparison |
| `PROVENANCE.txt` | Why a file is there and when it was produced |

<a id="fr-3-1"></a>

### 3.1 How figures are named

- **One continuous scheme: `F01`-`F37`.** Since 1.7.1 the number in the file
  name, the in-figure title, the card heading and this index is the same
  number. There are no gaps and no lettered suffixes: numbers retired by the
  1.6.0 reclassification were reassigned.
- **Families by folder.** `pipeline_cleaning/` holds F01-F16 (pipeline and
  detection figures, interleaved in build order) and F33-F37 (the reversal
  and clock-time families, added last); `research_ready/` holds F17-F32. Within
  `pipeline_cleaning/`, a detection figure (F06-F14) can therefore carry a
  higher number than a pipeline figure — generation order, not importance.
- **Two numbering systems, kept apart.** `F01`-`F37` is the pipeline's own
  numbering and is the only one used in prose and cross-references. The
  paper numbering (Methods 1-2, Results 3-13, Supplement S1-S24) is a default
  suggestion for a manuscript, mapped in the index above; the paper number
  appears only in each card's caption.
- **File names are stable.** Renaming touches the code, the figure index
  registry and any script of yours that reads these files, so the F numbers
  above are the only numbering in use. `figure_index.png` labels each thumbnail
  with its file name and a short caption.

<a id="fr-3-2"></a>

### 3.2 Choosing figures for the paper

> **For reference only.** The split below is a starting point, not a rule;
> which figures to use depends on your paper's story and the journal's limits.

The index's "Paper figure" column already reflects this default:

- **Methods, main text (2 figures).** F01 (Figure 1) — shows what the pipeline
  IS: stages, counts, the final classification breakdown. F17 (Figure 2) —
  shows what cleaning DID: non-destructive, only confirmed input errors
  modified. These two answer the reviewer's first two questions ("what did you
  do?" and "how invasive was it?") with no clutter.
- **Results, main text (pick 3–5 of the 11).** F19 (Figure 4, TST
  distribution) as the data-quality anchor; F24/F25 (Figures 9-10, perception
  bias) if subjective-versus-computed agreement is part of your story; F30
  (Figure 11, weekday vs weekend) or F31 (Figure 12, TIB composition) if
  timing regularity or composition matters; F32 (Figure 13, correlation
  matrix) if you reference metric interrelationships. Resist putting more than
  five in the main text — the rest reads better as supplement.
- **Supplement (everything else).** All `pipeline_cleaning/` figures (F02-F16,
  F33-F37) form the audit trail: put them in a supplement titled "Data quality
  and cleaning audit" and cite the set collectively from Methods with one
  sentence ("see Supplement S1 for the full audit trail"). The substance-use
  figures (F26-F29) belong with whatever substance-use analysis the paper
  reports, or in the supplement if none.

A minimal working set if page limits are tight: **F01 + F17 in Methods, F19 +
F24 + F32 in Results, the audit trail as a supplement.** Captions for every one
of these are at the end of its card in §4 or §5.

<a id="fr-4"></a>

## 4. Pipeline-cleaning figure cards (`pipeline_cleaning/`)

Every figure is documented as a self-contained card: what each part means, the
exact rules it is built from, what healthy data look like, what anomalies mean,
and a paper-ready caption.

<a id="f01-pipeline-record-flow"></a>

#### F01 · Pipeline Record Flow

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F01.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:937`

**Paper use** Methods, Figure 1

**What each part means** Vertical flow of 5 stages, each self-describing: Raw Load (all diary entries) → Parsed (entries with timestamps) → Auto-Corrected (AM/PM + order fixes) → Manual-Corrected (human review fixes) → Final Valid (usable for analysis). Each box = record count + % of total; two correction stages also show participant counts.

The key on the right of the figure lists every final record class with its count and a one-line definition. The full definitions are:

| Class | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Not Reported | Any of bed / sleep / awake / getup time is missing |
| Error (Reviewed) | Order broken (not `bed ≤ sleep ≤ awake ≤ getup`), `sleep = awake`, a gap > 7 h, or a sleep span > 24 h — reviewed and fixed |
| Equal Time | `bed == sleep` and/or `awake == getup` (difference < 0.01 h, about 36 s) with the order intact — a benign diary habit. (`sleep == awake` is an ERROR, not this.) |
| Unusual (Accepted) | Order intact but a gap > 3 h (bed→sleep or awake→getup) — odd but possible, reviewed and kept as-is |
| Clean | Order intact, no gap > 3 h |

First match wins, in the order above. A sixth class, Reasonable unusual, holds unusual patterns a reviewer marked as reasonable; it counts as valid. The subtitle gives the share of raw records entering analysis and the number of participants with at least one correction.

**Healthy look** The flow narrows gently from raw to valid. Clean is the biggest class in the side annotation, and Error + Unusual together stay under about 5%. The two correction stages show small counts — only genuinely broken records were fixed; everything else stays as reported.

**Anomaly →** A large Error/Unusual share usually means AM/PM confusion or a parsing problem upstream, not thousands of truly bad nights. Near-zero correction counts on data you know contains errors mean the detector missed rows.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **What is counted.** One row per raw diary entry (13,990 in the real run). The five boxes are successive stages: everything loaded, then entries that have timestamps, then entries fixed by rules (AM/PM and order fixes), then entries fixed by a human, then entries usable for analysis. Every percentage is out of the raw total.
- **How the side list is made.** Every final record gets exactly one class, checked top to bottom: not reported, error, equal time, unusual, clean. The first match wins. The exact rules are in the Terminology section, and the figure prints them next to each class.
- **The bottom line** ("x% of raw records enter analysis") is the share of raw entries that have all four timestamps and therefore computed sleep metrics.
- **Participants with a correction** counts participants who have at least one corrected record, out of all participants.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Why isn't Equal Time classified as an error?</summary>

A zero sleep latency (or getting up the moment you wake) is a plausible thing to report. The pipeline keeps `error` for records that are impossible as written: a broken order, or zero sleep.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What if both pairs are equal (bed = sleep and awake = getup)?</summary>

It is still `equal_time_ok`, recorded as `both_equal`.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What does 0.01 h mean for a reviewer?</summary>

Two timestamps that differ by less than about 36 seconds count as the same. The tolerance only absorbs floating-point rounding; it does not hide real differences.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why are almost 80% of the records "Not Reported"? Is that a problem?</summary>

It means those rows are missing at least one of the four times (for example, the diary was not completed that day). The pipeline never guesses a missing time. Whether it is a problem depends on your study design and expected response rate — compare it with what you expected.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Only 3 records are "Error (Reviewed)", but F17 shows 77 corrected records. Which is right?</summary>

Both. F01 classifies the FINAL data: errors that were fixed are no longer errors, so only 3 remain in that class. F17 counts the records that were changed along the way.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure 1.** Flow diagram tracing all raw diary entries through the five pipeline stages (raw load, timestamp parsing, algorithmic correction, manual correction, final valid output), with record counts and percentages at each stage. The side annotation reports the final record classification (clean, unusual accepted, error reviewed, equal-time benign, not-reported) and the proportion of participants who received at least one correction. TST = total sleep time; SOL = sleep onset latency.

<a id="f02-sleep-duration-post-correction"></a>

#### F02 · Sleep Duration Post-Correction

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F02.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:1422`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S1

**What each part means** Density curves of final sleep duration by record class (Clean / Unusual / Reasonable Unusual (accepted) / Manually Corrected / Error) after Steps 5–6.5. WHAT THIS ANSWERS: did the human corrections distort the overall sleep-duration distribution? (The corrected class's curve should overlap the clean curve.)

**Healthy look** One smooth peak around 6–8 hours, with nothing piled up at 0 or beyond 12 hours — the shape of normal night sleep. It also shows the human corrections did not distort the overall distribution.

**Anomaly →** A flat or two-humped curve means 12-hour and 24-hour time formats survived parsing; a spike at 0 means missing or zero-duration records slipped through.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **What is drawn.** A smoothed curve of the final `sleep_duration_h` (TST in hours) for each record class: Clean, Unusual, Reasonable Unusual (accepted), Manually Corrected and Error. Each curve is scaled to its own area, so compare shapes, not heights; the subtitle lists how many records each curve rests on.
- **Who is included.** Only records with a computed sleep duration, and only those five classes. Reasonable Unusual (accepted) is a record a reviewer marked "Reasonable unusual record": it is shown on its own, not folded into Unusual. A record that was manually corrected is shown as Manually Corrected, whatever its original class.
- **What it is for.** To check that human corrections did not distort the overall distribution: compare with F10, which shows the same kind of curve before any manual correction.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Why are there far fewer records here than the "usable for analysis" count in F01?</summary>

This figure draws only the Clean, Unusual, Reasonable Unusual (accepted), Manually Corrected and Error classes. Equal Time records (benign) and Not Reported records (no computed duration) are not in it.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why does the Unusual curve look different from the Clean one?</summary>

Unusual records were picked by a rule about odd gaps, so they are not a random sample. They need not look like the Clean records, and looking different is not evidence that they are wrong.

</details>

<details>
<summary>The Manually Corrected curve has extra bumps at the very short and very long ends. Is that a problem?</summary>

Manually corrected records were chosen because they were broken, so extreme durations are over-represented among them. It is worth opening those records one by one, but the bumps alone do not mean the corrections are wrong.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S1.** Density of final total sleep time (TST, hours) after all manual corrections were applied. Unimodal distributions centered on 6–8 h indicate healthy sleep durations; spikes at zero or > 12 h indicate residual parsing artifacts.

<a id="f03-flag-composition-stacked"></a>

#### F03 · Flag Composition Stacked

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F03.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:1491`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S2

**What each part means** Stacked histogram: x = sleep duration (h), y = number of records in that range, fill = `flag_severity` (see Terminology, above) under a legend titled "Data Quality". Shows whether quality problems cluster at extreme durations.

| Fill color | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Clean | 0 metric flags |
| Minor | 1 metric flag |
| Major | 2+ metric flags |

Not to be confused with `data_category` — a different classification system (see the Terminology section).

**Healthy look** In every duration bin the green (Clean) part is the biggest. Orange and red slivers (records with flagged metrics) appear mainly at the extremes — under about 3 h and over about 12 h — and at 0. That is expected: extreme durations are exactly what trip the sleep-efficiency, onset-latency and wake-time thresholds.

**Anomaly →** A wide orange/red band across the middle durations means a systematic parsing problem, not a handful of extreme records.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **What the colours mean.** The fill is `flag_severity`, not `data_category`: Clean (no metric flag), Minor (1 flag), Major (2 or more). A flag is one of: sleep efficiency below 70%, sleep onset latency above 1 h, wake after sleep onset above 1.5 h (set under `classification.flag_severity.*`).
- **What the bars are.** Each bar counts the records whose sleep duration falls in that range; the colours split each bar by severity.
- **What is cut off.** The x axis shows 0 to 16 h, and records with a duration of 0 or 20 h and above are left out.
- **The box in the corner** repeats the thresholds and the counts of Minor and Major records, so the figure can be read without this page.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>So this is about computed-metric flags, not timestamp errors?</summary>

Correct. F06 is about timestamp and format problems; F03 shows how many metric flags occur at each sleep duration. They are two different systems (`flag_severity` versus `data_category`).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why do the coloured slivers sit at the extremes?</summary>

Very short or very long sleep is exactly what tends to push sleep efficiency, onset latency or night waking past their thresholds, so flags naturally gather there. A flag there is a prompt to look, not a verdict.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Can I change the thresholds?</summary>

Yes, under `classification.flag_severity.*` in the config. The figure's corner box reads the current values, so it stays correct.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S2.** Stacked histogram of final sleep duration (hours), with bars colored by flag severity: Clean (no metric flags), Minor (one flag), Major (two or more flags from {SE < 70%, SOL > 1 h, WASO > 1.5 h}). Shows whether quality problems concentrate at extreme durations.

<a id="f04-extreme-sleep-durations"></a>

#### F04 · Extreme Sleep Durations

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F04.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:1601`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S3

**What each part means** Scatter: x = TST (h), y = sleep efficiency (%), restricted to extreme durations (< 4 h or > 10 h).

| Encoding | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Color | Data quality |
| Shape | Short vs long sleeper |
| Horizontal line | SE = 85% (poor-efficiency threshold) |

**Healthy look** The extremes are a small scatter of points. Short-sleep points (triangles) mostly sit at moderate sleep efficiency (roughly 60–95%) and long-sleep points (circles) at high efficiency, so these look like plausible unusual nights rather than arithmetic artefacts.

**Anomaly →** Many short-sleep points below 85% efficiency could be real insomnia or a measurement problem — look at those records one by one. Points sitting exactly at TST = 0 or 24 h point to a parsing failure.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **What is shown.** Only the extremes: records with TST under 4 h (triangles, "short") or over 10 h (circles, "long"). Everything in between is left out. Colour is the data-quality class.
- **The dashed line** at sleep efficiency 85% is a reading aid taken from the clinical rule of thumb. The pipeline's own flag uses 70% (`poor_efficiency_threshold_pct`), so a point can sit below 85% without being flagged.
- **Two sets of cut-offs.** 4 h and 10 h are this figure's own display cut-offs. They are looser than the pipeline's `duration_extreme` limits (under 3 h, over 12 h), which are a separate check.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Where do 4 h and 10 h come from?</summary>

They are display cut-offs chosen to show the tails of the distribution. They are not the pipeline's physiological limits (`duration_extreme`: under 3 h and over 12 h); do not mix the two.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Does a point below the 85% line mean the record is bad?</summary>

No. The line is a reference for reading the plot. A low efficiency with a short duration may be a real poor night, a measurement problem, or a diary entry that needs checking — the figure cannot tell which.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why are there so few points?</summary>

Only records outside the 4–10 h range are drawn, and most nights fall inside it. Few points is the expected, healthy picture.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S3.** Scatter of total sleep time (TST, hours) versus sleep efficiency (SE, %) restricted to extreme durations (< 4 h short, > 10 h long). Point shape encodes short vs long sleep; point color encodes record quality. The horizontal line marks the SE = 85% poor-efficiency threshold.

<a id="f05-flag-co-occurrence-heatmap"></a>

#### F05 · Flag Co-occurrence Heatmap

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F05.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:1688`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S4

**What each part means** Heatmap of how often two quality flags are raised on the same record, based on the final corrected data. Each axis lists the same four flags; each cell is the number of records on which both flags are TRUE, printed in the cell, with the colour running from pale to red as the count grows (square-root scale, legend "Co-occurrence Count").

| Axis label | Flag | Raised when |
|---|---|---|
| `poor_efficiency` | `flag_poor_efficiency` | Sleep efficiency is below `classification.flag_severity.poor_efficiency_threshold_pct` (default 70%) |
| `high_sol` | `flag_high_sol` | Sleep onset latency is above `classification.flag_severity.high_sol_threshold_hours` (default 1 h) |
| `high_waso` | `flag_high_waso` | Wake after sleep onset is above `classification.flag_severity.high_waso_threshold_hours` (default 1.5 h) |
| `sleep_calculation_issue` | `flag_sleep_calculation_issue` | Calculated and self-reported sleep onset latency differ by more than 30 minutes |

**Where the numbers come from** Not every flag rests on the same kind of value, which matters when you read the figure:

- `high_sol` uses the **calculated** SOL, not the self-reported one: the corrected bedtime and corrected sleep-onset time, `time_sleep_corrected − time_bed_corrected`, in minutes divided by 60.
- `high_waso` uses the **self-reported** WASO estimate (the minutes the participant gave, divided by 60).
- `sleep_calculation_issue` compares the calculated SOL with the self-reported SOL; it is the only flag that looks at the gap between the two.

**How to read a cell** Find the two flags on the axes and read the number in the cell. For example, the cell pairing `high_sol` with `sleep_calculation_issue` counts the records that have a long calculated SOL *and* disagree with the participant's own SOL answer. Those are the first records to look at, because the long SOL may come from a timestamp problem rather than from slow sleep onset. Each pair appears twice (see the precise rules), so read either copy.

Two questions come up often; the FAQ below answers them in full: [is high SOL self-reported or calculated?](#fig11-q-sol) and [what does `sleep_calculation_issue` mean?](#fig11-q-calc)

**Healthy look** Most cells are pale or absent, and no pair dominates. A few moderate cells are normal: a long calculated onset latency lowers sleep efficiency, and a large gap between calculated and reported SOL goes naturally with a high-SOL flag.

**Anomaly →** One cell far darker than the rest, or most pairs dark together, means one cause is setting off several flags at once (often a timestamp problem shared by many records, or thresholds that overlap by design). Check the records behind the dark cells, starting with `high_sol` × `sleep_calculation_issue`.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **What is counted.** Only records with a non-missing value in all four flag columns are used (`complete.cases`). A cell is the number of those records where both flags are TRUE.
- **Symmetric matrix.** The count of A with B equals the count of B with A, so every pair is drawn twice (once on each side of the diagonal). Read one triangle. The diagonal (a flag with itself) is not drawn.
- **Empty cells.** Pairs whose count is 0 are left out, not drawn as a zero cell. A blank cell means "never together", not "missing".
- **Colour scale.** Square-root, so that a few large counts do not flatten the small ones. Compare colours roughly; read the printed number for the exact count.
- **Data source.** The final corrected data (`clean_df`), the same data as F03 and F04.
- **Flags not used.** `flag_duration_extreme` and the three-level `flag_severity` label (Clean/Minor/Major — the `flag_severity` definition) are not part of this figure: neither is a plain TRUE/FALSE flag that can be counted in pairs.
- **When it is skipped.** If fewer than two of the four flag columns have complete data, or if no pair co-occurs on any record, the figure is not drawn and the reason is printed on the red block of `figure_index.png`.

</details>

**FAQ**

<a id="fig11-q-sol"></a>

<details>
<summary>Is a "high SOL" here self-reported or calculated?</summary>

**Calculated.** `flag_high_sol` uses `sol_h = self_diffcalc_sol_minutes / 60`, where `self_diffcalc_sol_minutes` is the corrected sleep-onset time minus the corrected bedtime, in minutes. The SOL the participant typed (`duration_totalmin_sol_estimate_am_mincalc`) is **not** used for this flag. It enters the figure only through `sleep_calculation_issue`, which compares the two. By contrast, `flag_high_waso` uses the self-reported WASO estimate.

Do not confuse it with `SELF_REPORTED_FLAG` from Step 8 (the file `flagged_records_self_reported.csv`). That is a different flag: it marks records whose self-reported values look implausible, for example a self-reported SOL over 120 min (or a very low TST/TIB ratio). It is not part of this figure.

</details>

<a id="fig11-q-calc"></a>

<details>
<summary>What does sleep_calculation_issue mean?</summary>

`flag_sleep_calculation_issue` is TRUE when the calculated SOL and the self-reported SOL differ by more than 30 minutes. It looks at SOL only, not WASO or total sleep time. Despite the name it does **not** mean a calculation bug; it means the two accounts of how long it took to fall asleep do not match. Typical causes are a timestamp error, a mistyped SOL (for instance a clock time entered in the minutes field), or ordinary perception bias.

Two things to know: if either value is missing the flag is FALSE (not NA), so "not flagged" does not mean the two agree. And the 30-minute cutoff is fixed in the code (`sleep_visualization.R`, `add_quality_flags()`); it is not a config key and does not appear on the Thresholds page.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Does a dark high_sol cell mean the participants really took a long time to fall asleep?</summary>

Not necessarily. In the validation data the calculated and the self-reported SOL can differ by up to about 75 minutes (see [Validation Methodology](validation-methodology.html)), so a high-SOL flag cannot tell a truly long onset from ordinary disagreement between the two sources. These flags are descriptive indicators for human review, not automated error signals.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why are some pairs missing?</summary>

Their count is 0 in this run. Pairs with no co-occurrence are not drawn.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why does the figure not appear in my output?</summary>

Either fewer than two flag columns had complete data, or no pair of flags occurred together. The reason is printed on the red block at the top of `figure_index.png`.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S4.** Co-occurrence of data quality flags in the final corrected data. Each cell gives the number of records on which both flags are present (poor efficiency: SE < 70%; high SOL: calculated SOL > 1 h; high WASO: self-reported WASO > 1.5 h; sleep calculation issue: calculated and self-reported SOL differ by more than 30 min). Only records with complete values on all four flags are counted; pairs that never co-occur are not drawn. Colour is on a square-root scale. Flags are descriptive indicators for review, not error classifications.

<a id="f06-error-category-distribution"></a>

#### F06 · Error Category Distribution

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F06.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:1878`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S5

**What each part means** Bar chart of auto-detection error/review categories with counts and % labels. Categories mirror `auto_error_desc` prefixes (Temporal / Metrics / Amount / Interval / Timestamp).

**Healthy look** One or two categories dominate (usually Metric Threshold or Temporal), and every category is small in absolute terms — the review queue is short and concentrated in a few causes.

**Anomaly →** Large Timestamp Format or Interval Format bars mean participants entered times in non-standard ways in bulk; check the parsing rules before reviewing records one by one.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **What the bars count.** Records flagged by the automatic check in Step 8, before any manual correction, grouped by the kind of problem. The kind comes from the prefix of the check's message: `[Temporal]` temporal issues, `[Metrics]` metric thresholds, `[Amount]` amount/input flags, `[Interval]` interval format, `[Timestamp]` timestamp format; anything else is "Other".
- **The subtitle** lists the metric rules feeding the Metric Threshold group: SOL above 120 min, sleep efficiency below 0 or above 100%, TST/TIB ratio below 0.5.
- **The two tables** under the bars explain the categories: the first lists each category with a severity and a plain description; the second counts records by their check result (for example SELF_REPORTED_FLAG, CLEAN).

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Why is it called "pre-correction"?</summary>

It answers "what did the raw data contain that needed attention?" — the load the pipeline had to absorb. F14 shows what is still flagged afterwards.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Does a record in a bar mean the record is wrong?</summary>

No. It means the automatic check wanted a human to look. Many flagged records are self-report-versus-computed disagreements that the pipeline deliberately keeps as data.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why is one bar so much taller than the others?</summary>

Usually one rule (here the metric thresholds) catches many records at once. A single dominant bar means a single common cause; check that cause first.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What is "Other Issue"?</summary>

It collects flagged records whose check message does not begin with one of the five known prefixes. In practice these are usually records flagged by the duration-reinterpretation check (message prefix `[DurationReinterp]`): an SOL or WASO value that might have been typed in the wrong format (for example minutes:seconds instead of hours:minutes).

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S5.** Bar chart of records flagged by the post-correction auto-detection pass, grouped into six review classes derived from the flag description: temporal issues, metric issues, amount/input flags, interval format errors, timestamp format errors, and other. Counts are pre-correction — they show the burden the pipeline had to absorb.

<a id="f07-adjacent-timestamp-gaps"></a>

#### F07 · Adjacent Timestamp Gaps

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F07.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:1961`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S6

**What each part means** Histogram of gap hours between adjacent diary events (bed→sleep, sleep→awake, awake→getup), **pre-correction raw times**. Negative gap = the later event's clock time precedes the earlier one. Vertical reference line at 0.

**Healthy look** Most gaps fall between +0.5 and +2 hours — positive means the events are in the expected order. A small negative tail is normal: a negative gap means the later event has an earlier clock time, the signature of an order error or a 12-hour AM/PM slip.

**Anomaly →** A large negative mass means widespread order errors that the normalizer will flip; two clusters near ±12 h point to a 12-hour-dial AM/PM habit.

**How to read it, in words** A tall red-band count in the Sleep -> Awake panel means many raw rows have sleep and awake times that look swapped or AM/PM-flipped; the normaliser and the review then deal with them. A count near zero in a panel means the pattern is rare in that pair of events. The number is about how often the pattern occurred in the raw entries, not about what is still open (see the FAQ below).

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **What a gap is.** For each of three neighbouring pairs — bed to sleep, sleep to awake, awake to getup — the gap is the later time minus the earlier time, in hours. It is computed on the raw (decoded) times, before any correction.
- **A negative gap** means the later event has an earlier clock time than the earlier one (for example awake at 01:00 but asleep at 23:00 in the same row). That is the raw signature of an order error or a 12-hour AM/PM slip.
- **The red band** marks gaps of −3 to −6 h, the range that defines the "AM/PM decode or field-swap candidate" definition used in the validation work; the count in the band is printed on it.
- **What the red `n=` label is.** There is one label per panel (Bed -> Sleep, Sleep -> Awake (TST), Awake -> Getup). It is the number of records in that panel whose raw, pre-correction gap is negative and between 3 and 6 hours in size (both ends included). It is counted live from the current run's data, never typed in, so it changes from run to run and from dataset to dataset; this is on purpose, so the label cannot drift from the real count.
- **Where the band comes from.** The 3 to 6 hour range is a definition fixed in the validation work (`validation/derive_timegap_candidates.R`): a reversal of that size is a typical signature of an AM/PM decode error or swapped fields. It is a definition for finding candidates, not a measured error rate.
- **What is outside the band.** Gaps reversed by less than 3 hours (small swaps) or by more than 6 hours are not counted in `n=`; other rules cover them (the shape notes above say which repair fits which pattern).
- **Adding up.** The per-panel numbers add up to the total number of candidates, and one record can appear in more than one panel.
- **How to read the shape.** A negative mass of roughly −1 to −3 h points to order swaps (repaired by the swap step); two clusters near ±12 h point to PM times typed as AM (repaired by the 12-hour flip).

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Why is this drawn before correction?</summary>

Because it shows what the raw entries looked like. After correction the negative gaps are mostly gone, so the picture would hide the problem the pipeline solved.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why are the three panels on different axes?</summary>

Each pair has its own typical size: bed→sleep and awake→getup gaps are usually under an hour or two, while sleep→awake is a whole night (about 6–10 h). Each panel is scaled to its own data.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Does a count in the red band mean that many records are wrong?</summary>

No. The number counts *candidates*, selected only by the size of the raw gap (negative, 3 to 6 hours). Some of them are real long gaps, or entries that run in the "wrong" direction out of habit; which ones are errors is decided by the cleaning rules and by review, not by this label.

It is also a picture of history: how often the pattern occurred in the raw entries. It does not show what is still unresolved after correction and review. For that, see the review status tables in [the manual-review cycle](interpreting-output.html#s-3) and the final record classification in [the run summary](interpreting-output.html#s-4).

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S6.** Histogram of the time gap (hours) between adjacent diary events (bed→sleep, sleep→awake, awake→getup) computed from raw, pre-correction timestamps. Negative gaps indicate the later event's clock time precedes the earlier one, the signature of order errors and 12 h AM/PM dial habits.

<a id="f08-detection-outcomes-heatmap"></a>

#### F08 · Detection Outcomes Heatmap

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F08.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:2034`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S7

**What each part means** A heatmap from the synthetic error-injection benchmark. Each row is an error type that was injected into clean records on purpose. Each column is what the pipeline did with it: `CORRECT` (fixed correctly), `FLAGGED_UNRESOLVED` (caught and handed to a human, not fixed), `MISREPAIRED` (fixed wrongly), `MISSED` (not detected), `NO_MATCH`. Each cell is the percentage of that error type's rows with that outcome. The subtitle gives the number of injected rows and categories.

**Healthy look** For each row, almost all of the colour sits in `CORRECT` or `FLAGGED_UNRESOLVED` — the error was either fixed correctly or caught and sent to a human — and `MISREPAIRED`, `MISSED` and `NO_MATCH` stay near 0. Some error types are only ever flagged and never auto-fixed (for example wrong-field entries); that is by design, because the pipeline flags what it cannot fix safely instead of guessing.

**Anomaly →** Colour in `MISREPAIRED` means the automatic fix was wrong — worse than leaving the record alone. Colour in `MISSED` means the error was not detected at all.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **Where the data come from.** The synthetic error-injection benchmark (`validation/synthetic/results/detection_outcomes_v4_current.csv`): known errors were injected into clean data, and the pipeline was run on the result. Because the right answer is known, each outcome can be labelled.
- **What a cell is.** For an injected error type, `n` is the number of injected rows; a cell is `count / n × 100`. Each row therefore adds up to about 100%.
- **The five outcomes.** `CORRECT` fixed correctly; `FLAGGED_UNRESOLVED` caught and handed to a human without a fix; `MISREPAIRED` fixed wrongly; `MISSED` not detected; `NO_MATCH` the injected row could not be matched one-to-one to a row in the pipeline output.
- **If the file is missing** from the working directory, the figure is skipped and the reason appears at the top of the figure index.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Why does a synthetic-injection figure belong in a QC folder?</summary>

It is the evidence that the detection numbers mean something: the detector is checked against known ground truth, whereas on real data the "correct" answer is unknowable.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Is FLAGGED_UNRESOLVED a failure?</summary>

No. It means the pipeline noticed the problem but did not want to guess a fix, so it left the decision to a person. For some error types (for example values typed into the wrong field) that is the intended behaviour.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Which colour would worry me most?</summary>

MISREPAIRED. A wrong automatic fix is worse than leaving the record alone, because it changes data without anyone noticing. MISSED is the second: the error stays in the data undetected.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Does this say how many errors my real data have?</summary>

No. It is a test on synthetic data with errors put in on purpose. It tells you how reliable each detector is, not how many errors your own data contain.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S7.** Heatmap from the synthetic benchmark in which known errors were injected into clean records. Rows are injected error types; columns are pipeline outcomes (correctly fixed, flagged for review, misrepaired, missed); each cell is the percentage of that error type's rows with that outcome.

<a id="f09-threshold-vs-measurement-noise"></a>

#### F09 · Threshold vs Measurement Noise

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F09.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:2081`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S8

**What each part means** Horizontal bars, one for each cleaning threshold that can be checked against a self-report (the SOL and WASO thresholds; thresholds with no self-report counterpart, such as sleep efficiency, are left out and the subtitle says how many). Bar length = threshold ÷ measurement noise, where the noise is the half-width of the 95% Bland-Altman limits of agreement between the self-reported value and the value the pipeline computes from the timestamps. Dashed lines mark 2× (borderline) and 3× (safe).

**Healthy look** Bars at 3× or longer: the threshold is well above the normal disagreement between self-report and computed values, so a record flagged by it is unlikely to be flagged by measurement noise alone. Between 2× and 3× is borderline.

**Anomaly →** A bar shorter than 2× means the threshold sits inside the typical measurement disagreement: records it flags may be flagged by noise alone, so treat that flag as a prompt to look, not as evidence of an error — and consider raising the threshold.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **What each bar is.** A cleaning threshold divided by the measurement noise. Only thresholds that can be checked against a self-report are drawn (the SOL and WASO thresholds); the subtitle says how many others were left out, such as sleep efficiency.
- **What "noise" means.** The self-reported value and the value the pipeline computes from the timestamps never agree exactly. Their typical disagreement is the half-width of the 95% Bland-Altman limits of agreement; that is the noise.
- **How it is graded.** At least 5× conservative, at least 3× safe, at least 2× borderline, under 2× inside the noise. The dashed lines are at 2× and 3×.
- **Live numbers.** It is computed from this run's data by `validate_thresholds()` (`R/bland_altman.R`), not from the synthetic benchmark.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Why compare thresholds to noise at all?</summary>

A threshold smaller than the measurement noise detects nothing real — it would flag pure noise. This figure shows how far above the noise each threshold sits.

</details>

<details>
<summary>A bar is under 2×. Must I change the threshold?</summary>

Not necessarily. It means records flagged by that threshold may be flagged by noise alone, so treat those flags as prompts to look rather than as evidence of error. Raising the threshold is one option; keeping it and reviewing the flagged records is another.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why are sleep efficiency and TST/TIB not shown?</summary>

They have no self-reported counterpart to compare with, so the noise cannot be estimated. The subtitle says how many thresholds were left out.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S8.** Each cleaning threshold divided by the Bland-Altman measurement noise (half-width of the 95% limits of agreement between self-reported and computed values). Dashed lines mark 2× (borderline) and 3× (safe).

<a id="f10-sleep-duration-pre-correction"></a>

#### F10 · Sleep Duration Pre-Correction

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F10.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:2152`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S9

**What each part means** Two overlaid density curves of sleep duration: green = a sample (up to 5,000) of records with no auto-detection flag; red = records the algorithm flagged for review. Pre-correction view: algorithm only, no manual corrections. The subtitle gives both sample sizes.

**Healthy look** The flagged (red) curve is broader or shifted — that is why those records were flagged — and it rests on far fewer records than the clean (green) curve.

**Anomaly →** Flagged and clean curves that look identical mean the flags are unrelated to duration; they come from timestamp or format rules.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **Two groups.** Green is a random sample (up to 5,000) of records with no automatic flag. Red is every record the automatic check flagged that has a usable sleep duration.
- **Before any manual fix.** This uses the algorithm's flags only; manual corrections are not applied, so the curve shows what the automatic check saw.
- **Compare with F02,** which shows the same kind of curve after human review.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Why is the green group only a sample?</summary>

There are far more unflagged records than flagged ones; drawing up to 5,000 keeps the curve readable without changing its shape. The subtitle gives both sample sizes.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Is it a problem that the two curves look alike?</summary>

Not necessarily, but it tells you the flags are not driven by sleep duration — they come from timestamp or format rules instead.

</details>

<details>
<summary>When is this figure not produced?</summary>

When no flagged record has a usable sleep duration. The top of the figure index then says so.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S9.** Density of sleep duration (hours) for records without auto-detection flags (green, random sample of up to 5,000) and records flagged for review (red), before any manual correction.

<a id="f11-error-timeline"></a>

#### F11 · Error Timeline

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F11.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:2238`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S10

**What each part means** Stacked columns, one per month, counting records that carry a temporal classification from Step 5/6: `order_error` (error) and the three "suspicious gap" types (`bed_sleep_suspicious`, `sleep_awake_suspicious`, `awake_getup_suspicious`). Counted per month because there are only a few dozen such records in total; a per-day area chart would draw slanted blocks between isolated dates.

**Healthy look** Small counts spread across the study period, with no single month dominating — the unusual patterns are occasional, not tied to one period.

**Anomaly →** A spike in one month points to a protocol change or a data-collection disruption; a cluster at the start points to a learning curve or unclear instructions.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **Which records.** Records that carry a temporal classification: an order error (`order_error`) or one of three "suspicious gap" types (bed→sleep, sleep→awake, awake→getup). Each needs a bed timestamp so it can be placed on the calendar.
- **Why monthly.** There are only a few dozen such records in total. A daily area chart would draw slanted blocks between isolated days and suggest a trend that is not there, so the figure counts per month.
- **Data source.** `corrected_ema_data`, where the classification lives. `clean_df` is the earlier frame from before the classification, so it does not have these columns.
- **A flag is not a verdict.** Most of these records were reviewed and kept as reported (see F17).

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>What would a spike in one month mean?</summary>

It suggests something changed around then — a protocol change, a technical problem, or a wave of new participants. Look at which pattern type the spike consists of and at the participants involved.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why are the columns different colours?</summary>

Each colour is a pattern type: `order_error`, `bed_sleep_suspicious`, `sleep_awake_suspicious`, `awake_getup_suspicious`. The legend under the plot names them.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Records of mine have no date. Are they missing from the plot?</summary>

Yes. A record without a bed timestamp cannot be placed on the calendar, so it is not drawn.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S10.** Number of records per month with a temporal-order error or a suspicious-gap pattern (Step 6 classification), by pattern type.

<a id="f12-common-error-patterns"></a>

#### F12 · Common Error Patterns

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F12.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:2329`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S11

**What each part means** Horizontal bars ranking the specific patterns found in the auto-detection review queue: temporal order error, unusual sleep pattern, SOL / sleep-efficiency / TST-TIB metric abnormal, **SOL exceeds bed-to-sleep window**, WASO estimate inconsistent, interval-format and timestamp-parse issues. A final bar, **"Other / unclassified"**, counts queued records that match none of the named patterns, so a reader can see what share the named patterns do not explain.

**Healthy look** A few named patterns cover most of the queue, and "Other / unclassified" is small — the detector's reasons are well described.

**Anomaly →** A large "Other / unclassified" bar means some detection rule has no matching label in this figure.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **What is ranked.** The queue of records the automatic check flagged, sorted by the specific pattern found in its message: temporal order error, unusual sleep pattern, SOL / sleep-efficiency / TST-TIB metric abnormal, SOL exceeds the bed-to-sleep window, WASO estimate inconsistent, interval-format and timestamp-parse issues.
- **"Other / unclassified".** Flagged records that match none of the named patterns. The bar is always drawn last, so you can see what share the named patterns do not explain.
- **When it is skipped.** If every flagged record is "Other / unclassified", or there is nothing in the queue (for example because everything was already reviewed), the figure is not drawn and the reason is listed at the top of the figure index.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>What does "SOL exceeds bed-to-sleep window" mean?</summary>

The self-reported time to fall asleep is longer than the time between the bedtime and sleep-onset timestamps, plus a small tolerance (`window_tolerance_minutes`, 15 min by default). The two reports contradict each other, so a person should look.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Is a large "Other / unclassified" bar bad?</summary>

It is a signal about this figure, not about your data: the detector raised reasons that this figure has no label for. It is worth finding out what they are.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Is this the same as F06?</summary>

They draw on the same flagged records but group them differently. F06 groups by the kind of check; F12 names the specific pattern inside each message.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S11.** Most common automatically detected patterns among records in the review queue; the last bar collects records that match no named pattern.

<a id="f13-top-participants-by-flag-rate"></a>

#### F13 · Top Participants by Flag Rate

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F13.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:2408`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S12

**What each part means** Bar chart: top 15 participants by algorithm-flagged record RATE (flags ÷ days), with PID labels.

**Healthy look** Rates are modest (under about 30%) and no single participant stands far above the rest — flags are spread thinly, not concentrated in one person's diary.

**Anomaly →** One participant above about 60% usually means a habit (for example always entering times on a 12-hour dial) or a recurring format mistake; open their raw entries and look at the pattern.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **What the rate is.** For each participant, the number of records flagged by the automatic check divided by the number of diary days that participant has. The 15 highest rates are shown, each labelled with `flags / days`.
- **Why a rate, not a count.** Participants are observed for different lengths of time. Five flags in 75 days (7%) is not the same as five flags in 5 days (100%).
- **What it is for.** To find people whose diaries are worth a look. The figure does not say the records are wrong.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Why is the bar height a percentage but the label shows two numbers?</summary>

The height is the rate in percent; the label repeats it with the raw `flags/days` so you can see how much data it rests on. A high rate on few days is weaker evidence than a moderate rate on many.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Is the top participant a problem?</summary>

Not automatically. A high rate usually means a habit (for example always entering times on a 12-hour dial) or a recurring format mistake. Open that person's raw entries and look at the pattern before deciding anything.

</details>

<details>
<summary>How is this different from F16?</summary>

This figure ranks by automatic-check flags (algorithm only, before manual review). F16 ranks by the final metric flags (`flag_severity`) of the corrected data.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S12.** The 15 participants with the highest auto-detected flag rate (flags per observed diary day), not raw flag counts, so participants with few diary days are not overrepresented.

<a id="f14-auto-detected-dashboard"></a>

#### F14 · Auto-Detected Dashboard

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F14.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:2510`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S13

**What each part means** Left text panel "Key Metrics": three numbers, each with its name under it — auto-detected (needs human review), manually corrected (human-reviewed and fixed), and total records. Right: pie of review_source classes (Temporal Issues / Metrics Issues / Amount/Input Flags / Interval Format Errors / Timestamp Format Errors / Other).

**Healthy look** Flagged records are far fewer than total records; the largest slice is usually Temporal or Metrics issues; the numbers match `correction_status_final.csv`.

**Anomaly →** Numbers that disagree with the CSV mean the ledger and table pipeline are out of sync; a large Amount/Input slice points to a substance-use coding problem.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **Left panel.** Three headline numbers, each named under it: records the algorithm flagged (needs human review), records already fixed by a human, and the total number of records.
- **Right panel.** A pie of the flagged records by review source: Temporal, Metrics, Amount/Input, Interval Format, Timestamp Format, Other. Each slice shows its count and share.
- **A consistency check.** The numbers should match `correction_status_final.csv`; the console also checks that no corrected record is still flagged.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Why is the flagged number not zero after all the manual work?</summary>

The flagged number is the open queue: records the automatic check flagged that have been neither corrected nor accepted by a reviewer. It reaches zero only when every flagged record has been dealt with. The "already corrected" number next to it counts the ones a person fixed.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What should I do if a slice is large?</summary>

Open the matching card: a large Metrics slice points to F09 (are the thresholds above the noise?), a large Amount/Input slice points to the substance-use coding (F26–F29), a large Temporal slice points to F07 and F11.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why is there a pie when pies are hard to read?</summary>

It has only a handful of slices and its job is to show one dominant source at a glance. For exact numbers use the counts printed on the slices or F06.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S13.** Key metrics panel (total records, flagged records, manually corrected records) alongside a stacked bar of the six review-source classes. Counts must match `correction_status_final.csv`.

<a id="f15-step-flag-ledger"></a>

#### F15 · Step Flag Ledger

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F15.png` — generated at `figure12_step_flag_table.R:15`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S14

**What each part means** Grid table: one row per pipeline step; columns are N (records in the run), DC:error / DC:unusual (`data_category`, Step 5), SEV:Minor / SEV:Major (`flag_severity`, Step 7), CFE:flag (`checkforerrors`, Step 8), MISentry (`field_misentry`, Step 1.5), Corrected and Suppressed. A grey "—" means "not computable yet at that step"; the first number in a column is where it is generated. The key under the table spells out every abbreviation, and the numbers are centered under their headers. Read it like the CSV ledger (§5) rendered as a figure.

**Healthy look** Each column's counts first appear at the step that computes it and then stay constant. From Step 6 on, the six `data_category` counts add up to `n_total`, and the three `flag_severity` counts add up to `n_total` from Step 7 on.

**Anomaly →** Counts that change after the step that first computed them mean the pipeline is unstable (see the validation rules in §5).

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **One row per pipeline step.** The columns are the five evaluation systems, each computed once at a fixed step: `DC` (`data_category`, Step 5), `SEV` (`flag_severity`, Step 7), `CFE` (`checkforerrors`, Step 8), `MISentry` (`field_misentry`, Step 1.5), plus Corrected and Suppressed.
- **A dash means "not computable yet".** The first number in a column is where it is generated; after that the counts should stay put.
- **The two identities worth checking.** From Step 6 on, the six `data_category` counts add up to the number of records; from Step 7 on, the three `flag_severity` counts do too. The rule list is in §5.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Why do the numbers stay the same in the later rows?</summary>

Each standard is computed once and never recomputed. If a number changes after the step that first produced it, something in the pipeline is unstable.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What is the difference between Corrected and Suppressed?</summary>

Corrected counts records whose data were changed. Suppressed counts flags a human reviewed and accepted, so they no longer need attention but the data were not changed.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What does the CFE:flag column count, and why is it not the same as F06?</summary>

From Step 8 on it counts the records in each outcome of the automatic check's summary (for example SELF_REPORTED_FLAG), which is the same table behind `correction_status_final.csv`. That summary is built before a person's accepted rows are withdrawn, so it still counts them (85 in a real run), and it classifies the duration-reinterpretation flags as clean (39). F06 counts the open queue instead -- the example numbers are from a 2026-09 run (226 vs 272); check your own run's console summary for current counts. Steps before 8 show a dash because the check has not run yet.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Where is the same information as a file?</summary>

`output/step_flag_ledger.csv` (see §5). This figure is that table drawn as a picture.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S14.** Per-step × per-standard × per-category record counts for the five evaluation systems (field mis-entry, data category, flag severity, duration extreme, check-for-errors). Each standard is computed once at a fixed pipeline step; counts must remain constant thereafter.

<a id="f16-participants-worth-a-second-look"></a>

#### F16 · Participants Worth a Second Look

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F16.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:2680`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S15

**What each part means** A table (not a bar chart) of the 20 participants with the highest flagged-record rate — participant ID, total records, and the Clean / Minor / Major percentages — for manual review prioritization; rows at 20% flagged or more are tinted orange, 50% or more red. The figure's subtitle defines Minor (1 flag) and Major (2+ flags) with the current thresholds.

**Healthy look** A short list, and no participant far above the rest.

**Anomaly →** A long list means a systemic issue affecting many participants, not individual behavior.

**What to do with this list** No, you do not have to re-check everything. The table only says whom to look at first. It changes no data and is not a completion criterion: whether the review is finished is decided by the review status tables for the error and unusual worksheets (see [the manual-review cycle](interpreting-output.html#s-3)), not by this table. It is worth a look when some rows are tinted orange (20% flagged or more) or red (50% or more), when the list is long, or before you treat the results as final, when it is a good idea to spot-check the top few rows.

To check one listed participant:

1. **See which flag drives the rate:** poor sleep efficiency, high SOL or high WASO. The defaults are efficiency below 70%, SOL above 1 hour and WASO above 1.5 hours (`classification.flag_severity.poor_efficiency_threshold_pct`, `high_sol_threshold_hours`, `high_waso_threshold_hours`). They come from the configuration, so your run may use other values; the figure's subtitle shows the ones in force.
2. **If it is mostly SOL,** remember that high SOL is calculated from the corrected bed and sleep times, not from the SOL the participant typed. Compare the two (the [F05 card](#f05-flag-co-occurrence-heatmap) explains `flag_sleep_calculation_issue`). A large gap between them is usually a descriptive difference, not an error; keep it.
3. **Check whether those records were already handled by a person:** the `human_review` and `has_correction` columns of the output, and `audit_disposition` in `cleaned_data_prepostcorrection.csv`. Records already handled do not need a second pass.
4. **If the timestamps themselves look wrong** (bedtime after sleep onset, or the order broken across midnight), send the record to review through the manual-review cycle. Otherwise leave it as it is and note your decision.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **Who is listed.** The 20 participants with the highest share of their own records flagged by `flag_severity` (Minor plus Major). The share is 100% minus the Clean percentage.
- **The colours.** Rows at 20% flagged or more are tinted orange, 50% or more red. In a healthy dataset no row is tinted.
- **Not a quality verdict.** A flag marks a record that differs from an automatic expectation, including self-report-versus-computed disagreements that the pipeline keeps on purpose.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>A participant has a high flag rate. Is their data wrong?</summary>

Not necessarily. The list says whose records are worth checking first; the verdict comes from looking at the records, not from this table.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Does a high rate mean we have to redo the cleaning?</summary>

No. A high rate means these participants' records are worth a look first; it does not mean the cleaning failed. The flags are descriptive: they include self-report-versus-computed disagreements that the pipeline keeps on purpose, and a person whose sleep latency is persistently long will appear in the list even when every entry is correct. Also, the high-SOL flag cannot tell a truly long SOL from ordinary reporting disagreement (see [F05](#f05-flag-co-occurrence-heatmap) and [Validation Methodology](validation-methodology.html)).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why is nobody coloured in my figure?</summary>

Colours start at 20% flagged. If every participant is below that, the table is working as intended — there is no one who stands out.

</details>

<details>
<summary>How is this different from F13?</summary>

F13 ranks by the automatic check's flags before manual review; this table ranks by the final metric flags (`flag_severity`) of the corrected data.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S15.** Ranked table of participants by flagged-record rate, for manual review prioritization. A high rate flags records worth hand-checking; it is not a verdict that the data are wrong.

<a id="f33-out-of-order-nights-by-mechanism"></a>

#### F33 · Out-of-Order Nights, by Mechanism

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F33.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:3293`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S20

**Title and subtitle** Title: *Nights with out-of-order times, by mechanism*. Subtitle lines: what the figure answers (when the four times fail bed ≤ sleep onset ≤ awakening ≤ get-up, which kind of slip is it), how to read a bar, and the count N.

**What each part means** One row per way a night's four self-reported times (bed, sleep onset, final awakening, get-up) can fall out of order, from `classify_reversals()`. Every row is always drawn, empty ones included, so a mechanism with no cases reads as 0 instead of vanishing. The bar is the number of nights; the right column is its share of all out-of-order nights. Rows that fit none of the listed forms are pooled in "Other forms".

| Colour | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Dark grey | Two times exchanged (bed and sleep onset, or wake and get-up) |
| Light blue | One time 12 h away (typically an AM/PM slip) |
| Dark blue | Two times moved together by 12 h (whole night) |
| Orange | Visibly wrong: awakening before bedtime, gaps within rounding, an impossible get-up value |
| Grey-blue | No simple explanation, or a form not listed |

**Healthy look** A small share of complete nights (a few percent), most of it in the first rows: exchanged times and a sleep-onset time 12 h early are the forms the correction step repairs on its own.

**Anomaly →** A tall bar for "Bed time 12 h early" or "Whole night shifted 12 h" is not a problem with the figure: the automatic correction rarely repairs these, so those nights depend on the review worksheets. A tall "No simple explanation" bar means the reversals are not an AM/PM or ordering habit and deserve a look at the raw entries.

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **What counts.** A night with all four times present whose order violates bed ≤ sleep onset ≤ final awakening ≤ get-up. The subtitle gives the count, the number of complete nights and the percentage.
- **How a row is assigned.** The smallest edit that restores the order and keeps the night plausible: exchange two fields, shift one by 12 h, or shift two by 12 h. Nights no edit explains are assigned by what is visibly wrong.
- **Get-up values that cannot be real.** These are counted in the figure but reported apart in the subtitle, because they are a field-value problem rather than a sequence problem.
- **Nothing is changed.** The figure reads the pre-correction columns; it does not alter data.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Is a reversed night the same as an error the pipeline flagged?</summary>

No. This figure classifies the order violation by its likely mechanism. Whether the night was flagged, corrected by the algorithm, or sent to review is shown in the other pipeline figures.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why show rows with zero nights?</summary>

So that two datasets can be compared row by row, and so that a form you might expect (for example "Wake and rise times swapped") is visibly absent rather than silently missing.

</details>

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S20.** Nights whose self-reported times are out of order (bed ≤ sleep onset ≤ final awakening ≤ get-up), by most likely mechanism. One row per mechanism, bar = number of nights, right column = share of all out-of-order nights. N and the percentage of complete nights are in the subtitle.

<a id="f34-clock-time-rule-outcomes"></a>

#### F34 · Clock-Time Rule Outcomes (SOL / WASO)

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F34.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:3355`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S21

**Title and subtitle** Title: *SOL / WASO entries read as a clock time or a mistyped duration*. Subtitle lines: what the figure answers (what Step 6.5 did with each reinterpreted entry), how to read a bar, and the count N.

**What each part means** One bar per outcome of the Step 6.5 clock-time rule, for the SOL and WASO entries the interval parser had reinterpreted (read as minutes and seconds, or `dd:00`). The number at the end of a bar is the count; colour is the field (blue SOL, orange WASO). Source: `output/duration_clock_rule_log.csv`, which lists every entry and what was done.

| Bar | What it means |
|---|---|
| Kept as minutes | Typed like `5:00` and read as 5 minutes; not changed |
| SOL recomputed from the clock time | The typed time was close to the person's own sleep onset and after bedtime; SOL = typed time minus bedtime |
| Set to missing | The typed value was the bedtime (SOL), or WASO looks like a clock time; the original text is kept |
| Left for review | Clock-like but the rule does not decide; the value stays as parsed and is still flagged |

**Healthy look** Mostly "Kept as minutes", a few recomputed, very few set to missing.

**Anomaly →** A large "Left for review" bar means many entries sit between the rule's tolerance and its window; that is the list a person has to read.

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S21.** SOL and WASO entries that looked like a clock time or a mistyped duration, by what the clock-time rule did with each. N is in the subtitle.

<a id="f35-sol-clock-like-entries-vs-own-times"></a>

#### F35 · SOL Clock-Like Entries vs Own Times

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F35.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:3388`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S22

**Title and subtitle** Title: *SOL entries typed like a clock time, against the person's own times*. Subtitle lines: what the figure answers (was the typed time the sleep onset or the bedtime), how to read a dot, and N with the rule's tolerance and window.

**What each part means** Each dot is a SOL entry typed like a clock time. The x axis is the typed time minus the person's own bedtime, the y axis the typed time minus their own sleep onset, both in minutes on a 12-hour dial (no AM/PM was typed). The dashed box is the rule's tolerance (vertical) and window (horizontal); dots inside it are recomputed. Green = recomputed, red = set to missing, grey = left for review.

**Healthy look** Dots near zero on the y axis and 0 to 60 on the x axis: the person typed about when they fell asleep.

**Anomaly →** Dots near zero on the x axis and away from zero on the y axis are people who typed their bedtime. Dots far from both axes are not explained by either time.

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S22.** SOL entries typed like a clock time, as the distance (minutes, 12-hour dial) from the person's own bedtime and sleep onset. The dashed box marks the clock-time rule's tolerance and window.

<a id="f36-reversal-forms-synthetic-test"></a>

#### F36 · Reversal Forms in a Synthetic Test

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F36.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:3440`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S23

**Title and subtitle** Title: *Out-of-order nights in a synthetic test, by form*. Subtitle lines: what the figure answers (for each kind of reversed night, how often the rules put the time back to the true value and how often they change it to something else), how the test was built, and the overall rate.

**What each part means** One row per form of reversal, sorted from best to worst handled. The bar is the share of injected rows put back to the true value (blue at 99% or more, vermillion below), the line is the Wilson 95% interval, and the right-hand column counts rows the rules changed to a value that is not the true one. These are synthetic diaries with known truth: the forms were injected into clean rows in the proportions seen in one real study, and the clean rows were checked for changes. Source: `reversal_injection_outcomes.csv` (shipped in `inst/extdata/`; produced with sleepcleanr 1.9.0).

**Healthy look** Exchanged times and a single sleep-onset or rise time 12 hours out sit at 100% with no wrong repairs.

**Anomaly →** A short bar with many "changed, but not to the truth" is a form the rules cannot repair: a bed time 12 hours out, a whole night shifted, an awakening before bed time. Those nights reach a person through the review worksheets; they do not fix themselves.

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S23.** Share of injected out-of-order nights put back to the true value, by form, in a synthetic test with the form mix of one real study. Bars: percent; lines: Wilson 95% intervals; right column: rows changed to a wrong value. Clean rows altered: 0 of 6,650.

<a id="f37-out-of-order-before-after"></a>

#### F37 · Out-of-Order Nights, Before and After

**File** `pipeline_cleaning/F37.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:3527`

**Paper use** Supplement, Figure S24

**Title and subtitle** Title: *Out-of-order nights in this study, before and after the corrections*. Subtitle: how many nights were out of order before (the bar length), how many are in order and plausible after, and what "plausible" means (SOL 0-300 min, time in bed 2-16 h, TST 0.5-12 h).

**What each part means** One bar per family of mechanism (the same classes as F33, grouped). The bar length is the number of nights out of order before the corrections; its colours are what the final data looks like for those nights: in order and plausible, in order but implausible, still out of order, or no corrected value. It reads the final `time_*_corrected` columns of this run. It does not say whether a night was fixed by the algorithm or by a person, and "in order" does not prove the value is the true one.

**Healthy look** Almost all of each bar is blue.

**Anomaly →** Vermillion at the end of a bar: those nights are still out of order in the final data and need a person.

**Paper caption**

> **Figure S24.** Nights whose self-reported times were out of order before correction, by family of mechanism, coloured by the state of the same night in the final data. Plausible: SOL 0-300 min, time in bed 2-16 h, TST 0.5-12 h.

<a id="fr-5"></a>

## 5. Research-ready figure cards (`research_ready/`)

<a id="f17-correction-impact"></a>

#### F17 · Correction Impact

**File** `research_ready/F17.png` — generated at `sleep_visualization.R:1091`

**Paper use** Methods, Figure 2

**Purpose** An audit of how much, and in which direction, corrections changed the data. It answers "how invasive was the cleaning?" — the figure's subtitle says so and explains how to read each panel.

**What each part means** Three panels in a row, tagged a–c: (a) TST delta lollipops — one row per modified record, x = ΔTST (min); (b) same layout for SOL; (c) identity scatter of TST-before vs TST-after (all records). Below them, a summary table of TST/SOL mean ± SD before vs after. The caption states how many of how many records were modified.

| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| <span style="color:#E69F00">●</span> Orange | Algorithmic correction |
| <span style="color:#0072B2">●</span> Blue | Manual correction |
| <span style="color:#BFBFBF">●</span> Gray, 3% opacity (panel C only) | Unchanged record — an almost invisible backdrop behind the corrected points |
| Dotted diagonal (panel C) | 1:1 "no change" reference line |

**When nothing was corrected** If no record was changed (a clean dataset, or the manual-correction files were not applied), panels A–C would be empty, so the figure shows one sentence — "No record was changed by a correction in this run (none needed, or the manual-correction files were not applied)" — plus the before/after table, whose rows are then identical.

**Healthy look** Most points sit on the dotted diagonal, the bars in the top panels are short and cluster near 0, and the before/after means in the table are close. That means the cleaning was non-destructive: it changed a few records, not the data as a whole.

**Anomaly →** Very long bars or a large share of corrected rows mean corrections are changing real data, not just fixing entry errors; a clear shift in the before/after means calls for asking why so much was "fixed".

<details>
<summary><strong>Precise rules</strong></summary>

- **Who is counted as "modified".** Each record has a status: `manual` if a human correction touched it, otherwise `algorithmic` if a rule changed it, otherwise `none`. A record is never both; manual wins.
- **What the top panels plot.** Only modified records, one row each, sorted by the size of the change. ΔTST = TST after − TST before (minutes), ΔSOL likewise. A negative bar means the correction shortened the value.
- **What "before" means.** The "before" values are recomputed from the raw parsed timestamps (TST = awake − sleep − WASO, SOL = sleep − bed); the "after" values are the pipeline's final numbers.
- **The scatter** plots before (x) against after (y) for all records. Unchanged records are drawn almost transparent, so they form a faint band on the diagonal behind the few coloured modified points.
- **The table** gives the mean and SD of TST and SOL before and after; the caption says how many of how many records were modified.

</details>

**FAQ**

<details>
<summary>Why does most of the data sit on the diagonal?</summary>

Corrections are non-destructive by design: only confirmed input errors are fixed (about 0.6% of records in the real run). Differences between self-report and computed values are kept as data, not smoothed away.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Can a faint point sit far from the diagonal?</summary>

Unchanged records should sit on the diagonal. A faint point off it means the "before" value (recomputed from the raw timestamps) and the "after" value (the pipeline's final number) differ for a record that was not marked as corrected. The figure cannot say why; open that record.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why do so many corrected records show exactly ±720 minutes?</summary>

720 minutes is 12 hours. An AM/PM flip changes a clock time by exactly 12 hours, which moves the derived duration by 12 hours too, so AM/PM fixes stack up at the same length.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Does a big bar mean the correction was wrong?</summary>

No. A big change usually means a big input error was fixed, such as a 12-hour slip. Whether a correction was right is decided in review, not by this figure; the figure shows how large the changes were.

</details>

<details>
